analysis.investment_thesis: KPI Green Energy trades at INR 448 versus a Graham Number of ~INR 256 (using EPS ≈ ₹21.75 and BVPS ≈ ₹134), a 75% premium to intrinsic value by my calculation — offering zero margin of safety. The business has never generated positive free cash flow, surviving entirely on debt and equity issuances, which is precisely the kind of speculative capital structure I refuse to own.
key_strengths: Six consecutive years of positive net profit (₹9 Cr → ₹325 Cr), providing an actual earnings track record
Interest coverage of ~7x (EBIT ₹564 Cr / Finance cost ₹79 Cr in FY25) is adequate
Revenue growth of 92.6% CAGR — the underlying business is clearly winning contracts
key_risks: FCF has been negative every single year (-₹88 Cr to -₹1,297 Cr), meaning reported profits are accounting entries, not cash in hand
D/E of 0.88 far exceeds my 0.5 limit; borrowings ballooned from ₹139 Cr (2020) to ₹2,533 Cr (2025) — a 18x increase in 5 years
P/B of 3.34 means you are paying ₹3.34 for every ₹1 of tangible net assets — dangerous in a capital-intensive industry
red_flags: Graham Number ~₹256 vs market price ₹448 — stock is 75% above intrinsic value by my formula
Free cash flow negative in all 6 years of data; FY25 FCF was -₹1,297 Cr — growth funded entirely by external capital
No dividend — in a capital-intensive utility, absence of dividends means shareholders receive no tangible return
CWIP surged to ₹709 Cr (2025) from near-zero — large unproductive asset base at risk if projects are delayed
analysis.detailed_analysis:
KPI Green Energy fails every quantitative screen I apply. The P/E of 20.6 exceeds my ceiling of 15; the P/B of 3.34 is more than double my maximum of 1.5. My Graham Number (√(22.5 × ₹21.75 EPS × ₹134 BVPS)) yields approximately ₹256, meaning the market demands a 75% premium over what the numbers justify. Debt/equity of 0.88 also breaches my 0.5 limit. The current ratio is not explicitly stated but the financing structure — ₹2,533 Cr in borrowings against ₹119 Cr cash — signals a business wholly dependent on the continued goodwill of lenders and equity markets.

The most damning fact is the cash flow record: free cash flow has been negative every year without exception, reaching -₹1,297 Cr in FY25. The ₹325 Cr net profit is real on paper, but the company simultaneously burned ₹1,505 Cr in capex and raised ₹1,807 Cr from financing. This is a growth machine funded by the capital markets, not a self-sustaining business. Mr. Market is pricing in a bright renewable energy future; I require proof of present value. The promoter holding of 49.5% and strong ROE of 19.7% are encouraging qualities, but they do not compensate for paying three times book for a cash-burning enterprise. Intelligent investors do not pay for hope.
